name: Elizabeth I
info: Elizabeth I, the last monarch of the House of Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603; her reign saw an English Protestant church established, the Spanish Armada defeated and a flowering of English drama.

facts.born: 7 September 1533 at Greenwich Palace; daughter of Henry VIII of the House of Tudor and his second wife, Anne Boleyn
facts.died: 24 March 1603 at Richmond Palace, aged 69, between two and three in the morning, after an illness and a severe depression; interred in Westminster Abbey
facts.role: Queen of England and Ireland from 17 November 1558 until her death in 1603; Supreme Governor of the Church of England from 1559
facts.known: the Elizabethan Religious Settlement; never marrying, as the "Virgin Queen"; the imprisonment and execution of Mary, Queen of Scots; the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588; the speech to the troops at Tilbury; the Elizabethan era of Shakespeare and Marlowe; the charter of the East India Company; 44 years on the throne

t: Declared illegitimate at two when her mother, Anne Boleyn, was executed, and imprisoned under her Catholic half-sister Mary, Elizabeth came to the throne in 1558 at the age of 25.

She established an English church with the monarch as supreme governor, never married or named an heir, kept Mary, Queen of Scots, captive for nineteen years before sanctioning her execution, and fought a long war with Spain.

Her 44 years on the throne gave England stability and a sense of national identity, though recent historians point to military failures, the tactics of her forces in Ireland and the economic troubles of her last years.
dyk: Elizabeth translated Latin and Greek authors throughout her life. A translation of the Annals of Tacitus in Lambeth Palace Library was confirmed as her own in 2019, after a detailed analysis of the handwriting and paper.
ev: Elizabeth is born at Greenwich Palace, the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn
After Wyatt's rebellion against her half-sister Mary she is imprisoned in the Tower of London and then held under house arrest at Woodstock
Mary dies on 17 November and Elizabeth becomes queen at the age of 25
A new Act of Supremacy makes her Supreme Governor of the Church of England, and an Act of Uniformity makes church attendance compulsory
Pope Pius V issues the bull Regnans in Excelsis, declaring her excommunicated and releasing her subjects from allegiance
Mary, Queen of Scots, held in England for nineteen years, is beheaded at Fotheringhay Castle
The Spanish Armada is dispersed by English fire ships off Gravelines, and Elizabeth addresses her troops at Tilbury
Elizabeth dies at Richmond Palace aged 69, and James VI of Scotland is proclaimed king of England

sections.early:
Elizabeth was born on 7 September 1533 at Greenwich Palace, the daughter of Henry VIII of England and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. Henry had annulled his marriage to Catherine of Aragon in order to marry Anne, hoping for a male heir, and at birth Elizabeth was heir presumptive. She was two years and eight months old when her mother was beheaded on 19 May 1536; she was then declared illegitimate and deprived of her place in the succession. Eleven days after the execution Henry married Jane Seymour, who died the next year shortly after the birth of a son, Edward. Henry restored Elizabeth to the line of succession when she was 10.

Her governess from 1537, Catherine Champernowne, later known as Kat Ashley, taught her French, Dutch, Italian and Spanish. Under the tutors William Grindal and, from 1548, Roger Ascham she progressed in Latin and Greek, and by the time her formal education ended in 1550 she was one of the best educated women of her generation.

Henry VIII died in 1547 and her half-brother became king as Edward VI at the age of nine. Elizabeth joined the household of Henry's widow, Catherine Parr, and her new husband, Thomas Seymour, the king's uncle. There Seymour engaged in romps and horseplay with the 14-year-old Elizabeth, entering her bedroom in his nightgown; some historians believe the crisis affected her for the rest of her life. She was sent away in May 1548. After Parr's death Seymour planned to marry her, and in January 1549 he was arrested; under interrogation Elizabeth would admit nothing. Seymour was beheaded on 20 March 1549.
sections.rise:
Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, aged 15. His will excluded both his half-sisters from the succession and named Lady Jane Grey, who was deposed after nine days. On 3 August 1553 the Catholic Mary rode into London with Elizabeth at her side. Mary ordered everyone to attend Catholic Mass, and Elizabeth, educated in the Protestant faith, outwardly conformed. When Mary announced in 1554 that she would marry Philip of Spain, many looked to Elizabeth as a focus for opposition.

After Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January and February 1554, Elizabeth was interrogated and on 18 March imprisoned in the Tower of London. She protested her innocence; it is unlikely that she had plotted with the rebels, though some were known to have approached her. The imperial ambassador Simon Renard argued that Mary's throne would never be safe while Elizabeth lived, but her supporters in the government convinced Mary to spare her in the absence of hard evidence. On 22 May she was moved to Woodstock Palace, where she spent almost a year under house arrest.

Once it was clear in 1555 that Mary would have no child, Elizabeth's succession seemed assured, and Philip himself began to cultivate her. Mary recognised her as heir on 6 November 1558 and died on 17 November. Elizabeth, aged 25, told her council at Hatfield that she meant to direct all her actions by good advice and counsel. She was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 15 January 1559. She came to depend heavily on a group of advisers led by William Cecil, whom she created Baron Burghley.
sections.deeds:
One of her first acts was a settlement of religion. The Parliament of 1559 legislated for a church based on the Protestant settlement of Edward VI, with many Catholic elements such as vestments. The Act of Supremacy, law from 8 May 1559, made her Supreme Governor of the Church of England, and an Act of Uniformity made attendance at church and the use of the 1559 Book of Common Prayer compulsory, though the penalties for failing to conform were not extreme. The heresy laws were repealed.

Her foreign policy was largely defensive. The Treaty of Edinburgh of July 1560 removed the French threat in Scotland. In August 1585, by the Treaty of Nonsuch, she promised military support to the Dutch rebels against Philip II, which began the Anglo-Spanish War. In 1588 the Spanish Armada, sent to ferry an invasion force from the Netherlands, was defeated by miscalculation, misfortune and an attack of English fire ships off Gravelines; at Tilbury Elizabeth told her troops that she had "the heart and stomach of a king". She knighted Francis Drake after his circumnavigation of the globe from 1577 to 1580.

Under Elizabeth England traded with Morocco and signed a treaty of commerce with the Ottoman Empire in 1580. Walter Raleigh claimed the territory of Virginia, and his colonists landed on Roanoke Island in 1585. On 31 December 1600 she granted a charter to the East India Company. The 1590s saw William Shakespeare and Christopher Marlowe reach their maturity, though the writers and builders of the age owed little to the Queen directly, who was never a major patron of the arts.
sections.opponents:
The gravest threat came from Catholic opposition gathered around her cousin Mary, Queen of Scots, whom Elizabeth detained in England from 1568. After the Catholic rising in the North in 1569, over 750 rebels were executed on Elizabeth's orders. In 1570 Pope Pius V declared her excommunicated and a heretic. From the Ridolfi Plot of 1571 to the Babington Plot of 1586, her spymaster Francis Walsingham assembled a case against Mary, who was beheaded on 8 February 1587. Elizabeth claimed she had not meant the warrant to be dispatched; the sincerity of her remorse has been questioned by contemporaries and historians. Missionary priests were executed for treasonable conduct, and repression of Catholics intensified in her later years.

In Ireland, Crown forces pursued scorched-earth tactics, burning the land and slaughtering man, woman and child; during the revolt in Munster in 1582 an estimated 30,000 Irish people starved to death. Elizabeth advised that the Irish, "that rude and barbarous nation", be well treated, but no remorse was shown when bloodshed served the Crown's purpose.

Parliament urged her to marry or name an heir, and she was often accused of irresponsibility for refusing. Her wars were criticised as half-hearted: she refused promised funds for her starving soldiers in the Netherlands, the English Armada of 1589 was a catastrophic defeat with 11,000–15,000 killed, wounded or dead of disease, and Walter Raleigh wrote that she "did all by halves". Some historians depict her as a short-tempered, sometimes indecisive ruler who enjoyed more than her fair share of luck.
sections.last:
The years after 1588 brought difficulties that lasted to the end of the reign. The conflicts with Spain and in Ireland dragged on, taxes grew heavier, harvests were poor, prices rose and the standard of living fell. Most of her leading councillors had died around 1590, and a bitter rivalry arose between Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, and Robert Cecil, son of Lord Burghley. Her own authority lessened: in 1594 she could not prevent the execution of her physician, Dr Roderigo Lopes, wrongly accused of treason by Essex. Her grants of monopolies to courtiers led to price-fixing and resentment, which she answered in her "Golden Speech" of 30 November 1601.

Elizabeth was fond and indulgent of Essex, and repeatedly gave him military posts despite his record of irresponsibility. After he deserted his command in Ireland in 1599 she had him placed under house arrest. In February 1601 he tried to raise a rebellion in London and was beheaded on 25 February; she knew that her own misjudgements were partly to blame.

Lord Burghley died on 4 August 1598. Since Elizabeth would never name a successor, his son Robert Cecil negotiated in secret with James VI of Scotland, who had a strong but unrecognised claim. Her health remained fair until the autumn of 1602, when a series of deaths among her friends plunged her into a severe depression. In March 1603 she fell ill. She died at Richmond Palace on 24 March 1603, aged 69, and a few hours later Cecil and the council proclaimed James king of England. After her funeral on 28 April she was interred in Westminster Abbey.
sections.legacy:
Many of her subjects lamented Elizabeth, but others were relieved at her death. By the 1620s, as expectations of James declined, there was a nostalgic revival of her cult: she was praised as a heroine of the Protestant cause and the ruler of a golden age, and her reign was idealised as a time when crown, church and parliament had worked in balance. That picture proved lasting. Her memory was revived during the Napoleonic Wars and adapted in the Victorian era to imperial ideology, and historians such as J. E. Neale in 1934 and A. L. Rowse in 1950 interpreted the reign as a golden age of progress and idealised the Queen personally.

Recent historians have taken a more complicated view. They point to military failures on land and at sea, to the tactics in Ireland that stain her record, and to a foreign policy that was cautious and gave very limited aid to foreign Protestants. The victory over the Armada was not a turning point in a war that continued for another sixteen years; peace with Spain was signed in 1604, a year after her death.

The church she established helped to shape a national identity and remains in place today, although strict Protestants of her day regarded it as a compromise; she did not wish, as Francis Bacon put it, to "make windows into men's hearts and secret thoughts". She was the first Tudor to recognise that a monarch ruled by popular consent, and she worked with parliament and trusted advisers, a style of government that her Stuart successors failed to follow. Her reign gave its name to the Elizabethan era.

summary: Elizabeth I, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, became Queen of England and Ireland in 1558 after imprisonment under her half-sister Mary. She settled the English church, never married, had Mary, Queen of Scots, executed and saw the Spanish Armada defeated in 1588. She died in 1603, the last of the Tudors, and was succeeded by James VI of Scotland.

J. B. Black, The Reign of Elizabeth: 1558–1603 (Clarendon, 1945)
Hugh Bicheno, Elizabeth's Sea Dogs: How England's Mariners Became the Scourge of the Seas (Conway, 2012)
Frederick Chamberlin, Elizabeth and Leycester (Dodd, Mead & Co., 1939)
Patrick Collinson, Elizabeth I (Oxford University Press, 2007)

The list is therefore [] as the guide says; the count of 3-6 could not be met from this file.
Death date: the article gives 24 March 1603 and explains that under the old calendar, with New Year on 25 March, she died on the last day of 1602; the modern convention (1603) is used.
The Armada: the article dates the fire-ship attack off Gravelines to midnight on 28-29 July (7-8 August New Style) and the Tilbury review to 8 August; no day is given in the profile.

The article says both that Elizabeth 'advised her commanders that the Irish, "that rude and barbarous nation", be well treated' and that 'she or her commanders showed no remorse when force and bloodshed served their authoritarian purpose'. The profile keeps both halves and puts the second in the passive ('no remorse was shown').
The Munster revolt of the Earl of Desmond is dated by the article 'in 1582' with 'an estimated 30,000 Irish people starved to death'; copied as given.
The English Armada figures (23,375 men and 150 ships; 11,000-15,000 killed, wounded or died of disease; 40 ships sunk or captured) are the article's.
'The first Tudor to recognise that a monarch ruled by popular consent' is the article's own unattributed judgement.
